lead: A Turing machine is the simplest machine with an unbounded tape, and it sets the limit of what any algorithm can do. This unit defines the machine, traces its instantaneous descriptions, designs machines for languages and integer functions, and compares variants. After it you can read a transition table, prove a language accepted, build a universal simulator, and state the Church-Turing thesis correctly.
about: This unit moves from the Turing machine as a concrete machine to its role as the general model of computation. Chapter 5.1 fixes the tape, head, states and instantaneous description. Chapter 5.2 turns configurations into language acceptance. Chapter 5.3 uses that acceptance test to design machines that compute integer functions. Chapter 5.4 compares multitape and nondeterministic versions. Chapter 5.5 encodes a machine and its input so one universal machine can simulate another. Chapter 5.6 states the Church-Turing thesis that ties these models to effective computability. Chapter 5.7, taught by only a few universities, shows how finite control can store symbols.

chapters.idea: A Turing machine is a finite control with one read/write head on an unbounded tape, and an instantaneous description records the whole tape, state and head position.
chapters.depth: Formal definition M=(Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q<sub>0</sub>, q<sub>accept</sub>, q<sub>reject</sub>); Γ holds tape symbols; blank □ is in Γ but not Σ; δ is a partial function Q×Γ → Q×Γ×{L,R}. Transition diagram arcs show read/write/move; transition table shows the same information. Instantaneous description α q β: α is the tape left of the head, q is the current state, β starts at the scanned cell. Yield relation ⊢ and ⊢*; halting configurations. Some syllabi call an instantaneous description a configuration.

figure.title: Turing machine parts
figure.aria: A finite control controls a read/write head that scans one cell of a tape; blank cells extend to the right.

chapters.example: Let M have δ(q<sub>0</sub>,0)=(q<sub>1</sub>,1,R), δ(q<sub>1</sub>,0)=(q<sub>2</sub>,0,R), δ(q<sub>2</sub>,□)=(q<sub>accept</sub>,□,L). For input 00, write the sequence of instantaneous descriptions.
chapters.trap: In an ID the state sits before the scanned symbol; do not put the state at the left end or add arbitrary blank cells.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: alphabets, strings and finite automata as a picture of finite control.
chapters.leave: Acceptance and language meaning to 5.2; multitape and nondeterministic definitions to 5.4; undecidability to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A Turing machine accepts a string when its run reaches the accept state; its language is the set of all such strings.
chapters.depth: Acceptance by final state: L(M)={w∈Σ* | q<sub>0</sub>w ⊢* α q<sub>accept</sub>β}. Reject state or no move means reject; a looping run accepts no string and rejects no string. Decider halts on every input; acceptor may loop. Contrast acceptor and decider. Mention L(M) is called recursively enumerable; the recursive versus recursively enumerable distinction is in Unit 6. Some syllabi call this the language of a TM.

figure.title: Acceptance test for strings containing 1
figure.aria: A flowchart scans right; a cell holding 1 goes to accept, a blank goes to reject, and 0 moves the head right.

chapters.example: Let M have δ(q<sub>0</sub>,0)=(q<sub>0</sub>,0,R), δ(q<sub>0</sub>,1)=(q<sub>accept</sub>,1,R), δ(q<sub>0</sub>,□)=(q<sub>reject</sub>,□,R). Trace input 001 and input 000; state whether M accepts.
chapters.trap: Acceptance means reaching the accept state, not merely stopping; a TM that loops has neither accepted nor rejected.
chapters.leave: Recursive and recursively enumerable languages to Unit 6; halting problem to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Turing machines are designed by small state routines, and integer functions are computed using unary tape codes.
chapters.depth: Design by routines: scan, mark, compare, shift. Integer functions use unary code 0^n for n; arguments separated by 1; output one unary block. Cover successor, addition, equality test and copying outline. Some syllabi call this TM as computer of integer functions.

figure.title: Unary addition on tape
figure.aria: Two tape rows show the separator 1 between two unary blocks removed and a third 0 added, changing 0010 into 000.

chapters.example: Design a TM for f(m,n)=m+n on unary numbers 0^m 1 0^n. Trace m=2, n=1: input 0010 must become 000.
chapters.trap: Unary representation: n is 0^n, not binary; the output must be one contiguous unary block.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.2: transition notation and acceptance test.
chapters.leave: Complexity of the computation to Unit 6; formal computable-function theory to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Multitape and nondeterministic Turing machines are convenient variants that recognize the same languages as the single-tape model.
chapters.depth: Multitape TM: k tapes, k heads, δ: Q×Γ^k → Q×Γ^k×{L,R}^k. Nondeterministic TM: δ returns a finite set of moves. Equivalence: both recognize exactly the recursively enumerable languages; single-tape simulation uses separators and head markers, O(t²) slowdown for t steps; nondeterministic simulation by BFS over configurations. Some syllabi call these variants or versions of TM.

figure.title: Two-tape Turing machine
figure.aria: One finite control drives two independent heads, each scanning its own tape.

chapters.example: Give a two-tape TM for L={0^n1^n | n≥1}. On input 0011, after reading all zeros, tape 1 holds 0011 and tape 2 holds 00; after reading all ones, tape 2 is erased and M accepts.
chapters.trap: Nondeterministic and multitape TMs do not recognize more languages than single-tape TMs; they only change convenience and speed.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 to 5.3: model, acceptance and design routines.
chapters.leave: Formal simulation proof details to exercises; undecidability to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A universal Turing machine reads a coded description of any Turing machine and simulates it on a given input.
chapters.depth: Universal TM U takes ⟨M,w⟩, decodes the transition table, keeps the simulated state and tape, and performs one move of M per cycle. U accepts iff M accepts; it loops if M loops. UTM shows a fixed machine can run any program; its acceptance language is recursively enumerable, not recursive (Unit 6). Some syllabi call this Universality of Turing Machine.

figure.title: Universal simulation
figure.aria: A universal machine reads a coded machine and input, sets the simulated state and tape, and accepts or rejects as the simulated machine would.

chapters.example: Let M accept strings ending in 1. U receives code(M) followed by 101. Explain the simulation: U reads code(M), starts simulated state q<sub>0</sub> on 101, scans to the final 1, and accepts.
chapters.trap: A UTM simulates M; it does not decide whether M halts. If M loops, U loops.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 to 5.4: notation, acceptance, variants and tape encoding.
chapters.leave: Halting problem, undecidability and Rice's theorem to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The Church-Turing thesis says every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine.
chapters.depth: Statement: every effectively computable function is computable by a TM. Evidence from lambda calculus, recursive functions and Post systems; all define the same class. Thesis, not theorem; cannot be proved, only supported. Some syllabi call it Church's thesis.

figure.title: Equivalent models of computation
figure.aria: Three formal models, lambda calculus, recursive functions and Turing machines, all lead to the same class of effectively computable functions.

chapters.example: The lambda term (λn.n+1) 5 reduces to 6. Use the Church-Turing thesis to conclude that a Turing machine computes f(5)=6.
chapters.trap: It is a thesis, not a theorem; one example or one model does not prove it.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.3: TM computation and integer functions.
chapters.leave: Formal proofs of equivalence of models to advanced reading; complexity classes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Finite control can remember a bounded amount of information by encoding it in state names, reducing tape work.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Finite control stores bounded information by naming states q<sub>ab</sub> for the last symbols a,b; use state tuples to simulate multiple tracks or remember a fixed number of cells. It cannot store an unbounded count. Examples: suffix recognition and marking two symbols.

figure.title: States store last two bits
figure.aria: A table lists four states q00 to q11, each name storing the last two input bits.

chapters.example: Design a TM that accepts strings over {0,1} ending in 01 by storing the last two bits in state names q00, q01, q10, q11. Trace input 1101; it ends in state q01, so accept.
chapters.trap: State storage is finite: states cannot remember an unbounded count such as how many 0s have been read.
chapters.leave: Unbounded memory to tape work; general multi-track simulation to 5.4.
